docs.title: AWS Organizations Policies
docs.text: Examples of Service Control Policies (SCPs) and Resource Control Policies (RCPs) to use as guardrails in an AWS organization. Each example explains what it blocks, why, and what to adjust before attaching it.

docs.title: Organizations Policies
docs.text: AWS Organizations lets you manage many AWS accounts from one place. Two of its features do most of the governance work: SCPs limit what your identities can do, and RCPs limit who can reach your resources. Used together, they are the base of a data perimeter.

docs.title: Differences
docs.text: SCP RCP Target IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the root user Resources in member accounts, such as S3 buckets and KMS keys Main goal Restrict what your identities can do Restrict who or what can access your resources External principals Not restricted Restricted Services All Supported services only (S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager, ECR, DynamoDB, CloudWatch Logs, Cognito and others) Default policy FullAWSAccess RCPFullAWSAccess (can't be detached) Effects Allow and Deny Deny only, with "Principal": "*" Not affected Management account, service-linked roles Management account, service-linked roles, AWS managed KMS keys

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Knowing how AWS combines these policies is what keeps you from locking yourself out of your own accounts. Every request starts as an implicit deny, and SCPs and RCPs never grant anything: they only set the maximum. Since FullAWSAccess and RCPFullAWSAccess allow everything, in practice only your Deny statements count.

The decision flow:

  1. Does any policy (SCP, RCP, identity, resource, permissions boundary or session policy) explicitly deny the action?
    • If yes: denied.
    • If no: go to step 2.
  2. If the resource is in a member account, do the RCPs from the root down to that account allow it?
    • If no: denied.
    • If yes: go to step 3.
  3. If the principal is in a member account, do the SCPs from the root down to that account allow it?
    • If no: denied.
    • If yes: go to step 4.
  4. Does the identity policy or the resource policy allow it? For cross-account access, both have to.
    • If no: denied by the implicit deny.
    • If yes: go to step 5.
  5. If there is a permissions boundary or session policy, does it allow it too?
    • If no: denied.
    • If yes: allowed.

Policies are inherited. A policy attached to an OU applies to every account below it, and nothing at a lower level can override a Deny from above.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep the management account for management only: no SCP or RCP applies there. Leave workloads out of it and delegate security services to a separate account.
  • Organize OUs by function, not by org chart: Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/Dev, Sandbox, Suspended. Attach broad guardrails at the root and specific ones at the OU level.
  • Use exception roles, not exception accounts: an ArnNotLike on aws:PrincipalArn with a single privileged role keeps exceptions small and easy to audit.
  • Match ARNs with ArnLike and ArnNotLike: StringNotEquals doesn't support wildcards, so arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin never matches and the exception silently stops working.
  • Combine statements: a root, OU or account takes up to 10 SCPs and 5 RCPs, and the default policies use one slot of each. Group related statements instead of creating one policy per control.
  • Roll out gradually: attach to a test account, then a test OU, then up the hierarchy. A broken policy at the root breaks every account at once.
  • Keep policies in code: manage them with Terraform, CloudFormation or Control Tower, and validate on every change.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A strict guardrail can block legitimate traffic. These tools help find out what happened, and ideally catch it before the policy is attached:

  • IAM Access Analyzer: aws accessanalyzer validate-policy --policy-type SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY --policy-document file://policy.json (or RESOURCE_CONTROL_POLICY) catches invalid actions, unknown condition keys and syntax errors. Before attaching data perimeter RCPs, also check the external access findings to see what is already shared outside the organization.
  • Service Authorization Reference: a condition key on an action that doesn't support it is not an error for IAM. The condition just never matches and the statement silently does nothing, or always applies with negated operators. The reference lists the keys of each action (also available as JSON), and scripts/validate_policies.py checks every example in this repository against it.
  • AWS CloudTrail: search for AccessDenied or UnauthorizedOperation. The error message says which policy type denied the request, for example with an explicit deny in a service control policy or in a resource control policy.

  • IAM policy simulator: evaluates the SCPs attached to an account without running anything, which is useful for actions you wouldn't try for real, like organizations:LeaveOrganization. Attach the SCP to a test OU and run:

    aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/developer \
  --action-names organizations:LeaveOrganization cloudtrail:StopLogging iam:CreateUser \
  --context-entries "ContextKeyName=aws:PrincipalArn,ContextKeyValues=arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/developer,ContextKeyType=string" \
                    "ContextKeyName=aws:RequestedRegion,ContextKeyValues=us-east-1,ContextKeyType=string" \
  --query 'EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]' --output table

    Use a role with broad permissions, so any explicitDeny comes from the SCP, then repeat with the exception role and expect allowed. A few things to keep in mind:

    • It doesn't evaluate RCPs, or SCPs that aren't attached yet.
    • It doesn't fill in aws:PrincipalArn. Without it in --context-entries, ArnNotLike exceptions always match and the exception role shows up as denied.
    • Keys used only in SCPs, like aws:RequestedRegion, can only be set from the CLI.
    • Results can differ from real requests. Confirm with one when you can, for example aws ec2 run-instances --dry-run.

docs.title: Other policy types
docs.text:
Some controls are better enforced by other policy types in AWS Organizations. They configure the service directly instead of blocking API calls, and they also apply to service-linked roles.

docs.title: About
docs.text: SCPs set the maximum permissions available to IAM users and roles in an organization. Whatever an identity's own policies say, the SCP decides which services and actions are available at all.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Deny list, not allow list: keep FullAWSAccess attached and write SCPs with only Deny statements. With an allow list you have to maintain every action each team needs, and anything you forget stops working.
  • The root user is covered: in member accounts, SCPs also restrict the root user. They are the main way to keep root credentials from being used.
  • Global services live in us-east-1: a Region restriction has to exempt IAM, Organizations, CloudFront, Route 53 and the other global services, or they stop working. The Region example has the full list.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text:
Value Quota Maximum number of policies attached to a root, OU or account 10 Maximum size of a policy document 10,240 characters Maximum number of SCPs in the organization 10,000

Whitespace counts toward the size, for RCPs too. The console strips it when saving, but the CLI and SDKs don't, so minify the JSON before deploying from code:

jq -c . policy.json

docs.title: About
docs.text: RCPs set the maximum permissions on resources in an organization, whoever is calling, including principals from outside it. They let you enforce a data perimeter centrally, even when a bucket policy or key policy allows too much.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Check service support: RCPs only apply to supported services, and an action from any other service simply has no effect. The list keeps growing, so check it before writing a new policy.
  • Watch out for outsiders: RCPs also apply to principals from other AWS accounts. An exception for arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin lets in a role named admin from someone else's account too. Pair those policies with the identity perimeter, or use account IDs instead of *.
  • Leave AWS services alone: add "BoolIfExists": {"aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"} when a policy shouldn't affect service principals, such as CloudTrail delivering logs to a bucket.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text:
Value Quota Maximum number of policies attached to a root, OU or account 5 Maximum size of a policy document 5,120 characters Maximum number of RCPs in the organization 2,000

RCPFullAWSAccess takes one of the 5 slots and can't be detached, so there are only 4 left for your own policies.

docs.title: RCP Examples
docs.text:
Every RCP statement must be a Deny with "Principal": "*". RCPFullAWSAccess stays attached and counts toward the limit of 5 RCPs per entity.

Before using them:

  • Replace the placeholders: o-xxxxxxxxxx (organization ID), 222222222222 (trusted third-party account), my-github-org, 203.0.113.0/24 (corporate CIDR) and role names such as admin and iac-deploy.
  • Each example is a separate policy for readability. With only 4 free RCP slots per entity, merge statements from several examples into one policy.
  • RCPs only apply to supported services. An action from an unsupported service in an RCP has no effect.
  • RCPs don't apply to resources in the management account, to calls made by service-linked roles, or to AWS managed KMS keys.
  • Unlike SCPs, RCPs are evaluated for principals outside your organization too. An exception like arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin also matches a role named admin in someone else's account. Pair those policies with the identity perimeter, or use account IDs instead of *.
  • Review IAM Access Analyzer external access findings before attaching data perimeter policies. They show which resources are already shared outside the organization.

docs.title: Enforce the identity perimeter
docs.text:
Reference: AWS data perimeter examples

Only principals from your organization (or from the trusted account 222222222222) can access your resources or assume your roles, even if a bucket policy, key policy or role trust policy says otherwise. This is the RCP that stops a misconfigured resource policy from becoming a data leak.

  • AWS service principals are not affected (aws:PrincipalIsAWSService). They are handled by the confused deputy policy.
  • sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML are left out because federated users don't belong to an organization. Use the OIDC policy for those.
  • Tag a resource with dp:exclude:identity = true to exempt it, for example a bucket that intentionally shares data with a partner. Protect that tag with an SCP so only the platform team can set it.
  • ELB access logs in older Regions are delivered by an AWS-owned account. If you use them, add that account to aws:PrincipalAccount.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnforceOrgIdentities",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "aoss:*",
        "cognito-idp:*",
        "dynamodb:*",
        "ecr:*",
        "kms:*",
        "logs:*",
        "s3:*",
        "secretsmanager:*",
        "sqs:*",
        "sts:AssumeRole",
        "sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage",
        "sts:GetAccessKeyInfo",
        "sts:GetFederationToken",
        "sts:GetServiceBearerToken",
        "sts:GetSessionToken",
        "sts:SetContext"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-xxxxxxxxxx",
          "aws:PrincipalAccount": [
            "222222222222"
          ],
          "aws:ResourceTag/dp:exclude:identity": "true"
        },
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Enforce confused deputy protection
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

When an AWS service accesses your resources with its service principal (for example CloudTrail writing to a bucket or SNS sending to a queue), someone else's resource could trick the service into acting on yours. That is the confused deputy problem.

This policy only lets service principals act on your resources when the request comes from your organization or from 222222222222. Requests without aws:SourceAccount are not affected, since there is nothing to compare.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnforceConfusedDeputyProtection",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "aoss:*",
        "cognito-identity:*",
        "cognito-idp:*",
        "dynamodb:*",
        "ecr:*",
        "kms:*",
        "logs:*",
        "s3:*",
        "secretsmanager:*",
        "sqs:*",
        "sts:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "aws:SourceOrgID": "o-xxxxxxxxxx",
          "aws:SourceAccount": [
            "222222222222"
          ],
          "aws:ResourceTag/dp:exclude:identity": "true"
        },
        "Null": {
          "aws:SourceAccount": "false"
        },
        "Bool": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "true"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Enforce the network perimeter
docs.text:
Reference: AWS data perimeter examples

Denies access unless the request comes from a VPC endpoint owned by your organization or from the corporate CIDR. Stolen credentials used from a laptop on the internet stop working.

This one breaks things easily, so it ships opt-in: it only applies to principals tagged dp:include:network = true. Tag roles gradually and remove the condition once everything is covered.

  • Requests made by AWS services on your behalf (aws:ViaAWSService) and by service principals are not affected.
  • aws:ec2-infrastructure is the role EC2 uses for things like EBS encryption with KMS.
  • Use dp:exclude:network = true on a principal or resource to exempt it.
  • Only add services that support aws:VpceOrgID. For the others the key is never present, so every request outside the corporate CIDR would be denied, even through your own VPC endpoints.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnforceNetworkPerimeter",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "cognito-identity:*",
        "ecr:*",
        "kms:*",
        "s3:*",
        "sqs:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "NotIpAddressIfExists": {
          "aws:SourceIp": "203.0.113.0/24"
        },
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "aws:VpceOrgID": "o-xxxxxxxxxx",
          "aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network": "true",
          "aws:ResourceTag/dp:exclude:network": "true"
        },
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false",
          "aws:ViaAWSService": "false"
        },
        "ArnNotLikeIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws:ec2-infrastructure"
        },
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network": "true"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Require HTTPS
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

Denies any request to your resources over plain HTTP.

All AWS API endpoints have required TLS 1.2 or later since February 2024, so a separate policy denying s3:TlsVersion below 1.2 no longer adds anything. If you need TLS 1.3, add a statement with "NumericLessThan": {"s3:TlsVersion": "1.3"} and test your clients first.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnforceSecureTransport",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "aoss:*",
        "cognito-identity:*",
        "cognito-idp:*",
        "dynamodb:*",
        "ecr:*",
        "kms:*",
        "logs:*",
        "s3:*",
        "secretsmanager:*",
        "sqs:*",
        "sts:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:SecureTransport": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Isolate production resources
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

The identity perimeter treats every account in the organization the same. This adds a boundary inside it: resources in the production OU can only be accessed by principals from the production OU or the security OU. A compromised dev account can't read prod data even if a bucket or key policy allows it.

Attach it to the production OU. Paths come from aws organizations list-parents and follow the format o-xxxxxxxxxx/r-xxxx/ou-xxxx-xxxxxxxx/. External principals have no aws:PrincipalOrgPaths, so they are denied as well. If prod shares data with a third party, add an exception for that account or tag the resource. If deployment pipelines run in a separate OU and write to prod resources (artifacts in S3, images in ECR), add that OU's path too.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "IsolateProductionOU",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "dynamodb:*",
        "ecr:*",
        "kms:*",
        "logs:*",
        "s3:*",
        "secretsmanager:*",
        "sqs:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ForAllValues:StringNotLikeIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalOrgPaths": [
            "o-xxxxxxxxxx/r-xxxx/ou-xxxx-prod0000/*",
            "o-xxxxxxxxxx/r-xxxx/ou-xxxx-secu0000/*"
          ]
        },
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "aws:ResourceTag/dp:exclude:identity": "true"
        },
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Restrict OIDC federation to trusted providers
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

GitHub Actions uses the same issuer for every customer. A role trust policy that checks only aud lets any GitHub repository in the world assume it. This policy rejects GitHub tokens that don't come from my-github-org, regardless of what the trust policy says.

  • EnforceGitHubOrg: the Null check limits the statement to GitHub tokens. Without it, every other OIDC provider (EKS IRSA, GitLab, Terraform Cloud) would be denied too.
  • DenyBuiltInWebIdentityProviders: blocks Google, Facebook, Login with Amazon and Cognito identity pools as direct web identity providers. Remove cognito-identity.amazonaws.com if you use Cognito identity pools.

Other SaaS providers with a shared issuer (GitLab.com, Terraform Cloud, Pulumi, Vercel) need the same treatment. AWS keeps a list with ready-made statements.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnforceGitHubOrg",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotLikeIfExists": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-github-org/*"
        },
        "Null": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "false"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyBuiltInWebIdentityProviders",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:FederatedProvider": [
            "accounts.google.com",
            "cognito-identity.amazonaws.com",
            "graph.facebook.com",
            "www.amazon.com"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny unauthenticated Cognito identity pool access
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

Guest access in a Cognito identity pool hands out AWS credentials to anyone who knows the pool ID, which is usually embedded in a frontend. This denies credentials for unauthenticated identities in every pool.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyUnauthenticatedIdentityPoolAccess",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "cognito-identity:GetCredentialsForIdentity",
        "cognito-identity:GetId",
        "cognito-identity:GetOpenIdToken"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "Null": {
          "cognito-identity-unauth:IdentityPoolArn": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny SSE-C uploads
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

S3 has encrypted every new object with SSE-S3 by default since January 2023, so a policy requiring the encryption header is no longer needed.

The real risk is SSE-C (customer-provided keys). Ransomware campaigns have used stolen credentials to rewrite objects with SSE-C using a key only the attacker has. Since April 2026, S3 disables SSE-C by default on new buckets, and on existing ones in accounts that never used it. It can still be turned back on per bucket, and accounts that already had SSE-C objects kept their settings. This RCP closes it everywhere, whatever the bucket configuration says.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenySSECUploads",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "Null": {
          "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Limit presigned URL lifetime
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

Presigned URLs can be valid for up to 7 days and work for anyone who has the link. This denies requests whose signature is older than 1 hour (3600000 ms), which limits how long a leaked URL stays useful.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyOldPresignedUrls",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "NumericGreaterThan": {
          "s3:signatureAge": "3600000"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Protect S3 bucket security settings
docs.text:
Only the admin and iac-deploy roles can change bucket policies, bucket ACLs, ownership controls, Block Public Access, encryption, versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle and replication.

Lifecycle and replication are included because both are used in attacks: a lifecycle rule can expire every object in a day, and replication can copy data to a bucket the attacker controls. s3:BypassGovernanceRetention is there too, so objects under Object Lock in governance mode can't be deleted early.

Object ACL actions are left out on purpose. Uploads with an x-amz-acl header (CloudTrail, ELB logs and many cross-account writers send bucket-owner-full-control) need s3:PutObjectAcl and would break. Disable ACLs with BucketOwnerEnforced instead.

Combine with the identity perimeter so roles with the same names in other accounts are also blocked.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyS3SecuritySettingChanges",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "s3:BypassGovernanceRetention",
        "s3:DeleteBucketPolicy",
        "s3:PutBucketAcl",
        "s3:PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration",
        "s3:PutBucketOwnershipControls",
        "s3:PutBucketPolicy",
        "s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock",
        "s3:PutBucketVersioning",
        "s3:PutEncryptionConfiguration",
        "s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration",
        "s3:PutReplicationConfiguration"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/iac-deploy"
          ]
        },
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Protect KMS keys
docs.text:
Reference: AWS RCP examples

  • DenyKeyDeletion: deleting or disabling a key makes everything encrypted with it unreadable. Only the admin role can do it.
  • DenyLockoutSafetyBypass: a key policy saved with the lockout safety check bypassed can leave the key with no one able to manage it.
  • DenyGrantsForNonAWSResources: grants give access to a key without showing up in the key policy, which makes them a quiet way to keep access. Only grants created by AWS services for their own resources (EBS, RDS and others) are allowed.
  • DenyShortDeletionWindow: a key scheduled for deletion can be recovered until the waiting period ends. This forces the maximum of 30 days, for everyone, so there is time to notice.
  • DenyDeletingKeysInUse: KMS tracks when each key was last used. Nobody, not even admin, can schedule the deletion of a key that encrypted or decrypted anything in the last 90 days, which stops both ransomware and deleting the wrong key. Disabling is left out on purpose: it can be undone, and during an incident it's how you cut off a compromised key. Some keys are used rarely (an EBS volume only uses its key when attached), so treat a long idle period as a hint, not as proof the key can go.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyKeyDeletion",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "kms:DeleteCustomKeyStore",
        "kms:DeleteImportedKeyMaterial",
        "kms:DisableKey",
        "kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        },
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyGrantsForNonAWSResources",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "kms:CreateGrant",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "kms:GrantIsForAWSResource": "false",
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyShortDeletionWindow",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "NumericLessThan": {
          "kms:ScheduleKeyDeletionPendingWindowInDays": "30"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyDeletingKeysInUse",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "NumericLessThan": {
          "kms:TrailingDaysWithoutKeyUsage": "90"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLockoutSafetyBypass",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "kms:CreateKey",
        "kms:PutKeyPolicy"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": {
          "kms:BypassPolicyLockoutSafetyCheck": "true"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny immediate secret deletion
docs.text:
By default a deleted secret can be restored for 7 to 30 days. ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery skips that window and the secret is gone for good, which is what ransomware and careless cleanup scripts do. This denies it for everyone, so a deleted secret can always be recovered.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyForceDeleteSecret",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "secretsmanager:DeleteSecret",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": {
          "secretsmanager:ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery": "true"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Protect security tags
docs.text:
When access is based on tags (ABAC) or the data perimeter uses dp:* tags, removing a tag can remove a restriction. This denies removing DataClassification, ManagedBy and any dp:* tag, except by the admin role.

  • S3 is not included. s3:PutBucketTagging replaces the whole tag set and aws:TagKeys lists the tags being kept, not the ones being removed, so the check can't be expressed reliably.
  • RCPs only cover supported services. For EC2, Lambda, RDS and others, use the same statement in an SCP (without Principal).
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenySecurityTagRemoval",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": [
        "dynamodb:UntagResource",
        "ecr:UntagResource",
        "kms:UntagResource",
        "logs:UntagResource",
        "secretsmanager:UntagResource",
        "sqs:UntagQueue"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ForAnyValue:StringLike": {
          "aws:TagKeys": [
            "DataClassification",
            "ManagedBy",
            "dp:*"
          ]
        },
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        },
        "BoolIfExists": {
          "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: SCP Examples
docs.text:
All examples follow a deny list strategy: FullAWSAccess stays attached and each policy only adds Deny statements.

Before using them:

  • Replace the placeholders: o-xxxxxxxxxx (organization ID), 111111111111 (account ID), 222222222222 (trusted third-party account), 203.0.113.0/24 (corporate CIDR), vpc-0123456789abcdef0 (your VPC) and the role names admin, security, network, finops and iac-deploy.
  • Each example is a separate policy for readability. With 10 SCPs per entity (FullAWSAccess takes one), merge statements from several examples into one policy.
  • arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin matches a role named admin in any account of the organization. If the exception role lives in a single account, use its account ID instead of *.
  • Exceptions by role name are only safe if nobody else can create or change a role with that name. Attach Protect critical IAM roles with every exception role in it before relying on any other policy here.
  • To exempt an IAM Identity Center permission set, match the generated role: arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/*AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_*.
  • If you use AWS Control Tower, add arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution to the exceptions of policies that touch CloudTrail, Config, IAM roles or Regions. Otherwise account enrollment and baseline updates fail.
  • SCPs don't apply to the management account or to service-linked roles.
  • Attach to a test OU first and watch CloudTrail for AccessDenied before moving the policy up the hierarchy.

docs.title: Deny account contact changes and closure
docs.text:
Contact information is how AWS reaches you about security events and how account recovery works. Changing it is a common step in account takeover. The same policy blocks closing the account from inside it.

The management account can still update member account contacts through the Account Management API, since SCPs don't apply there.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyAccountSettingsChanges",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "account:CloseAccount",
        "account:DeleteAlternateContact",
        "account:PutAlternateContact",
        "account:PutContactInformation"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny enabling or disabling Regions
docs.text:
Opt-in Regions should only be turned on by the platform team. An enabled but unmonitored Region is a good place to hide resources.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyRegionOptInChanges",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "account:EnableRegion",
        "account:DisableRegion"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny leaving the organization
docs.text:
An account that leaves the organization is no longer subject to its SCPs, RCPs or consolidated billing. This is one of the first SCPs AWS recommends attaching.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLeaveOrganization",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "organizations:LeaveOrganization",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny access to unapproved Regions
docs.text:
Reference: AWS SCP examples

Denies every request outside us-east-1 and sa-east-1. Global services are listed in NotAction because their endpoints live in us-east-1 and would otherwise break when us-east-1 isn't in the approved list.

Notes:

  • Include the home Region of IAM Identity Center and AWS Control Tower in the approved list.
  • If you use Control Tower, its Region deny control does the same thing and is maintained by AWS.
  • New global services show up over time. If something breaks with AccessDenied on us-east-1, check whether its prefix needs to go into NotAction.
  • Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference sends requests to other Regions in the same geography, which a plain Region deny blocks. DenyBedrockOutsideApprovedRegions handles that: Bedrock calls to other Regions are only allowed through us.* inference profiles. Use the prefix of your geography, and keep in mind that global.* profiles can route to any commercial Region.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyUnapprovedRegions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "NotAction": [
        "a4b:*",
        "acm:*",
        "aws-marketplace-management:*",
        "aws-marketplace:*",
        "aws-portal:*",
        "bedrock:InvokeModel",
        "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream",
        "budgets:*",
        "ce:*",
        "chime:*",
        "cloudfront:*",
        "config:*",
        "cur:*",
        "directconnect:*",
        "ec2:DescribeRegions",
        "ec2:DescribeTransitGateways",
        "ec2:DescribeVpnGateways",
        "fms:*",
        "globalaccelerator:*",
        "health:*",
        "iam:*",
        "importexport:*",
        "kms:*",
        "mobileanalytics:*",
        "networkmanager:*",
        "organizations:*",
        "pricing:*",
        "route53:*",
        "route53domains:*",
        "route53-recovery-cluster:*",
        "route53-recovery-control-config:*",
        "route53-recovery-readiness:*",
        "s3:GetAccountPublic*",
        "s3:ListAllMyBuckets",
        "s3:ListMultiRegionAccessPoints",
        "s3:PutAccountPublic*",
        "shield:*",
        "sts:*",
        "support:*",
        "trustedadvisor:*",
        "waf-regional:*",
        "waf:*",
        "wafv2:*",
        "wellarchitected:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": [
            "us-east-1",
            "sa-east-1"
          ]
        },
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyBedrockOutsideApprovedRegions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "bedrock:InvokeModel",
        "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": [
            "us-east-1",
            "sa-east-1"
          ]
        },
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/us.*",
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny root user access
docs.text:
Reference: AWS SCP examples

Blocks every action taken with root credentials in member accounts. Root sessions are hard to attribute to a person and the root password reset flow is a takeover path.

Sessions opened through centralized root access (sts:AssumeRoot, from the management account or a delegated admin) carry the aws:AssumedRoot key and are not blocked. That keeps root-only tasks possible, such as removing an S3 bucket policy that locks everyone out.

With centralized root access enabled you can also delete the root credentials of member accounts. Keep this SCP anyway for accounts that still have them.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyRootUser",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:root"
        },
        "Null": {
          "aws:AssumedRoot": "true"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny IAM users and long-term credentials
docs.text:
Access keys and console passwords for IAM users are the most common source of leaked AWS credentials. Use IAM Identity Center for people and roles for workloads, and block the creation of long-term credentials.

iam:CreateServiceSpecificCredential covers CodeCommit, Keyspaces and long-term Amazon Bedrock API keys.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLongTermCredentials",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "iam:CreateAccessKey",
        "iam:CreateLoginProfile",
        "iam:CreateServiceSpecificCredential",
        "iam:CreateUser",
        "iam:DeleteAccountPasswordPolicy",
        "iam:UpdateAccountPasswordPolicy",
        "iam:UpdateLoginProfile"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny identity provider changes
docs.text:
A new identity source is a back door: whoever controls it can get into the account without touching IAM users or roles. This covers the three ways to add one:

  • SAML and OIDC providers in IAM
  • IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchors (any certificate signed by the anchor's CA can get credentials)
  • IAM Identity Center account instances (sso:CreateInstance), a separate Identity Center that lives inside a member account and outside the central one
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyIdentityProviderChanges",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "iam:AddClientIDToOpenIDConnectProvider",
        "iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider",
        "iam:CreateSAMLProvider",
        "iam:DeleteOpenIDConnectProvider",
        "iam:DeleteSAMLProvider",
        "iam:RemoveClientIDFromOpenIDConnectProvider",
        "iam:UpdateOpenIDConnectProviderThumbprint",
        "iam:UpdateSAMLProvider",
        "rolesanywhere:CreateTrustAnchor",
        "rolesanywhere:EnableTrustAnchor",
        "rolesanywhere:UpdateTrustAnchor",
        "sso:CreateInstance"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Protect critical IAM roles
docs.text:
This is the policy that makes every exception in this project safe. The other SCPs and RCPs exempt roles by name (admin, security, network, finops, iac-deploy), and a name is all it takes: anyone who can create a role called network and attach a policy to it gets past the network SCP. So every exception role, plus the roles the platform depends on (cross-account access, StackSets, Control Tower, Identity Center, AWS Backup), is locked here. Only admin and the StackSets execution role, which deploys the baseline, can create or change them. If you add an exception role to any policy, add it here too.

  • DenyCriticalRoleChanges: creating, deleting, editing the trust policy or changing the permissions of these roles.
  • DenyPassingCriticalRoles: passing one of these roles to an EC2 instance or a Lambda function you control is as good as assuming it. iac-deploy and the AWS Backup role are left out because pipelines and backup plans legitimately pass them to CloudFormation and AWS Backup.
  • ProtectPlatformPolicies: locking a role isn't enough if its permissions come from a customer managed policy anyone can edit, since a new policy version changes what the role can do. This covers policies under the /platform/ path, so create the platform's policies with it (aws iam create-policy --path /platform/ ...).

Accounts created through Organizations or Control Tower get OrganizationAccountAccessRole or AWSControlTowerExecution from the service itself, which this policy doesn't affect. To enroll an existing account in Control Tower, create AWSControlTowerExecution with the admin role.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyCriticalRoleChanges",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "iam:AttachRolePolicy",
        "iam:CreateRole",
        "iam:DeleteRole",
        "iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary",
        "iam:DeleteRolePolicy",
        "iam:DetachRolePolicy",
        "iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary",
        "iam:PutRolePolicy",
        "iam:TagRole",
        "iam:UntagRole",
        "iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy",
        "iam:UpdateRole",
        "iam:UpdateRoleDescription"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/security",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/network",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/finops",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/iac-deploy",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyPassingCriticalRoles",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "iam:PassRole",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/security",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/network",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/finops",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole",
        "arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ProtectPlatformPolicies",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "iam:CreatePolicyVersion",
        "iam:DeletePolicy",
        "iam:DeletePolicyVersion",
        "iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion",
        "iam:TagPolicy",
        "iam:UntagPolicy"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::*:policy/platform/*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Require a permissions boundary on roles
docs.text:
Lets application teams create their own roles without being able to create one more powerful than allowed. Every role they create or change must have the workload-boundary policy as its permissions boundary.

  • RequireBoundary: creating, deleting or changing a role (its policies or its trust policy) is denied unless that role has the boundary. iam:PermissionsBoundary refers to the boundary of the target role, so this also stops teams from touching roles that don't have one, such as the platform roles. UpdateAssumeRolePolicy is the important one: without it, a team could edit the trust policy of a platform role and assume it.
  • DenyBoundaryRemoval: the boundary can't be removed.
  • ProtectBoundaryPolicy: the boundary policy itself can't be edited.

Create workload-boundary in every account before attaching. The StackSets execution role is exempted so the baseline can deploy the boundary and the platform roles. If another pipeline creates platform roles without a boundary, add its role to the exceptions. The boundary only limits roles; to keep teams from passing existing powerful roles to services, keep Protect critical IAM roles attached as well.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "RequireBoundary",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "iam:AttachRolePolicy",
        "iam:CreateRole",
        "iam:DeleteRole",
        "iam:DeleteRolePolicy",
        "iam:DetachRolePolicy",
        "iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary",
        "iam:PutRolePolicy",
        "iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "iam:PermissionsBoundary": "arn:aws:iam::*:policy/workload-boundary",
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyBoundaryRemoval",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ProtectBoundaryPolicy",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "iam:CreatePolicyVersion",
        "iam:DeletePolicy",
        "iam:DeletePolicyVersion",
        "iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::*:policy/workload-boundary",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Control outbound identity federation
docs.text:
Reference: IAM outbound identity federation

With outbound identity federation, AWS principals call sts:GetWebIdentityToken to get a signed JWT and use it to authenticate to other clouds and SaaS. It removes stored API keys, but it also means any role with that permission can authenticate to services outside AWS.

  • DenyEnablingOutboundFederation: only the admin role can turn the feature on in an account.
  • RestrictTokenAudience: tokens can only be issued for the listed audiences. Replace them with your external services.
  • LimitTokenLifetime: tokens are valid for at most 5 minutes.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyEnablingOutboundFederation",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "RestrictTokenAudience",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "sts:GetWebIdentityToken",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ForAnyValue:StringNotLike": {
          "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": [
            "https://api.example.com",
            "api://AzureADTokenExchange"
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "LimitTokenLifetime",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "sts:GetWebIdentityToken",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "NumericGreaterThan": {
          "sts:DurationSeconds": "300"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny Identity Store changes when users come from an IdP
docs.text:
Reference: AWS SCP examples

When IAM Identity Center gets its users and groups from Okta, Entra ID or Google through SCIM, the IdP is the only source of truth. Nobody should create a user or add someone to a group directly in Identity Center. That's exactly what an attacker with access to the Identity Center admin account would do to give themselves a permission set while staying invisible in the IdP.

SCIM provisioning uses its own token, not IAM, so it keeps working. Attach this to the account that is the delegated administrator for Identity Center. SCPs don't apply to the management account, so if Identity Center is administered from there, move it to a delegated admin first.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyIdentityStoreChanges",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "identitystore:Create*",
        "identitystore:Delete*",
        "identitystore:Update*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Deny disabling security services
docs.text:
Keeps detection and audit tooling running after the baseline is in place. Only the security role, used by the security team and its automation, can change these services.

Sid Protects DenyCloudTrail Trails and CloudTrail Lake event data stores DenyConfig Recorder, delivery channel, rules, aggregators, remediation DenyGuardDuty Detector, filters (auto-archive), trusted IP lists, membership DenySecurityHub Hub, standards, controls, automation rules, membership DenyAccessAnalyzer Analyzers and archive rules that hide findings DenyMacie Macie session and membership DenyInspector Inspector scanning and membership DenyEventBridge Rules that route security alerts (replace security-alerts-*)

If you use an organization trail and Control Tower, part of this is already enforced, but the SCP also covers trails and settings created outside them. Security Hub, GuardDuty and Inspector policies in Organizations turn these services on in every account; this SCP keeps anyone from weakening them afterwards.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyCloudTrail",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "cloudtrail:DeleteEventDataStore",
        "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail",
        "cloudtrail:PutEventSelectors",
        "cloudtrail:StopEventDataStoreIngestion",
        "cloudtrail:StopLogging",
        "cloudtrail:UpdateEventDataStore",
        "cloudtrail:UpdateTrail"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/security"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyConfig",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "config:DeleteAggregationAuthorization",
        "config:DeleteConfigRule",
        "config:DeleteConfigurationAggregator",
        "config:DeleteConfigurationRecorder",
        "config:DeleteDeliveryChannel",
        "config:DeleteEvaluationResults",
        "config:DeleteOrganizationConfigRule",
        "config:DeleteRemediationConfiguration",
        "config:DeleteRetentionConfiguration",
        "config:DeleteServiceLinkedConfigurationRecorder",
        "config:PutConfigRule",
        "config:PutConfigurationAggregator",
        "config:PutConfigurationRecorder",
        "config:PutDeliveryChannel",
        "config:PutOrganizationConfigRule",
        "config:PutRemediationConfigurations",
        "config:PutRetentionConfiguration",
        "config:StopConfigurationRecorder"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/security"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyGuardDuty",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "guardduty:AcceptAdministratorInvitation",
        "guardduty:ArchiveFindings",
        "guardduty:CreateFilter",
        "guardduty:CreateIPSet",
        "guardduty:CreatePublishingDestination",
        "guardduty:DeclineInvitations",
        "guardduty:DeleteDetector",
        "guardduty:DeleteFilter",
        "guardduty:DeleteIPSet",
        "guardduty:DeleteMembers",
        "guardduty:DeletePublishingDestination",
        "guardduty:DeleteThreatIntelSet",
        "guardduty:DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount",
        "guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount",
        "guardduty:DisassociateMembers",
        "guardduty:StopMonitoringMembers",
        "guardduty:UpdateDetector",
        "guardduty:UpdateFilter",
        "guardduty:UpdateIPSet",
        "guardduty:UpdateMalwareScanSettings",
        "guardduty:UpdatePublishingDestination",
        "guardduty:UpdateThreatIntelSet"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/security"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenySecurityHub",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "securityhub:BatchDeleteAutomationRules",
        "securityhub:BatchDisableStandards",
